item.title: Sri Lanka hopes to fully utilize Rs.2,000bn capital spending next year
item.dc:creator: Shihar Aneez
item.description: Cabinet Spokesman admits 2026 capital investment can't be fully utilized
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – The Sri Lankan government has adjusted its procurement cycles for development projects with the hope of utilizing the full Rs. 2,000 billion capital expenditure planned for next year, Cabinet Spokesman Nalinda Jayatissa said.

The island nation’s successive governments have failed to utilize the capital spending every year due to delays in approvals, tender process and procurements.

President Anura Kumara Dissanayake’s government has spent only less than 25 percent of the allocated Rs. 1,340 billion in the first nine months of the year, Finance Ministry officials have said.

“Spending 100 percent might not be possible in this year due to various technical reasons. In some places there were issues with tenders; in some places there were issues in the procurement process,” Jayatissa, also the minster of health and media, told reporters at the weekly Cabinet media briefing.

He said the government, however, has urged the ministries not to wait until January of next year to initiate these development projects.

“If you plan to start in January, you will only be able to actually get it underway around May,” he said.

“Now you know that funds will be allocated. The plans that respective ministries submitted to the Ministry of Finance knows about those plans. They have an idea of how much money will be spent. Accordingly, several steps including preparing plans, preparing estimates, and initiating procurement activities can be carried out even before the budget is passed.”

“(Ministries can) carry out the procurement activities, and wait until the budget is passed only to award the contract.”

“Once the budget is passed this time on December 14th, and after the Speaker signs it, generally within the month of December there is the ability to know the amount of money allocated to one’s ministry. Then, awarding can be made starting even from the first week of January, if needed.”

“It is that very process that we have granted approval for across all ministries. It is along with that that we expect to spend this 2,000 billion.”

Sri Lanka’s chronic failure to utilize its full budgetary allocations for capital investment reflects deep-rooted structural inefficiencies in public financial management and project execution, analysts and economists say.

They warn of lower economic growth in the future if the government fails to implement its planned capital investment projects.

The government has repeatedly said most of the spending occurs in the last quarter of the year.

Year after year, bureaucratic delays, protracted procurement disputes, politicized project selection, and a lack of technical expertise within line ministries leave a significant portion of capital expenditure unspent on the Treasury books.

This capital under-utilization carries severe long-term repercussions for the island’s economic trajectory.

By failing to deploy allocated funds into critical infrastructure such as transport networks, modernized power grids, and digital public systems, Sri Lanka suffers from lower productivity growth and worsening structural bottlenecks as well as a decline in overall gross domestic product (GDP) potential.

In a fragile post-default macroeconomic climate, this persistent shortfall also sends a negative signal to international development partners and private investors.

It demonstrates an institutional inability to absorb capital effectively, thereby stalling the very structural transformation required to safely out-grow a historic debt burden.

President Dissanayake last month promised to change the process to fast-track the spending. (Colombo/November 10/2026)

ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka’s rupee closed at 332.33/40 to the US dollar spot on Tuesday, from 332.53/59 the previous day, while bond yields closed lower, dealers said.

A bond maturing on 15.09.2029 closed at 10.80/90 percent, down from 10.90/98 percent.

A bond maturing on 01.08.2030 closed at 11.00/03 percent, down from 11.07/12 percent.

A bond maturing on 01.12.2031 closed at 11.12/15 percent.

A bond maturing on 15.12.2032 closed at 11.50/55 percent, down from 11.65/70 percent.

A bond maturing on 15.10.2034 closed at 11.92/97 percent, down from 12.10/15 percent.

A bond maturing on 15.08.2036 closed at 12.15/20 percent, down from 12.40/50 percent. (Colombo/Nov10/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka Cabinet approves $200mn ADB loan for MSMEs
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: The Department of External Resources has concluded formal loan negotiations with the ADB to acquire the funds.
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT — Sri Lanka’s cabinet has approved entering into an agreement with the Asian Development Bank (ADB) to obtain a 200 million US dollar loan to support micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs).

The facility will finance ‘Sub-program 1’ of the Sector Development Program, which focuses on building a robust and inclusive financial ecosystem for MSMEs.

The Department of External Resources has concluded formal loan negotiations with the ADB to acquire the funds.

The 200 million dollar loan will be drawn from the ADB’s ordinary capital resources and is divided into two equal tranches of 100 million US dollars each.

One tranche will serve as policy-based lending, while the other provides financial intermediation lending.

The financing falls under a broader framework approved on March 16, 2026, to conduct negotiations for up to 620 million US dollars across five sub-programs to support Sri Lanka’s reform agenda aligned with the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) Extended Fund Facility.

Responding to questions from journalists on why Sri Lanka is securing 200 million dollars after seeking approval for 620 million dollars, cabinet spokesperson Nalinda Jayatissa clarified:

“Approval has been granted for the entire 620 [million]. Accordingly, depending on how negotiations progress and based on the case we present, the loan is disbursed,” Jayatissa said.

Jayatissa noted that discussions were held to secure the 200 million dollar loan under two distinct repayment frameworks.

The 100 million dollar policy-based component carries a 12-year repayment period with a three-year grace period.

The remaining 100 million dollar financial intermediation component has a 15-year repayment period alongside a five-year grace period. (Colombo/Nov10/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka shares jump 2.75-pct on lower oil prices, US election tariff hopes
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: Easing global pressures and lower oil prices helped lift market sentiment
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka’s Colombo Stock Exchange closed sharply higher on Tuesday, CSE data showed, with the benchmark All Share Price Index moving up 2.75 percent.

The ASPI was up 592.02 points at 22,123.39, while the more liquid S&P SL20 was up 3.66 percent, or 224.97 points, at 6,368.12.

Easing global pressures and lower oil prices helped lift market sentiment, Raynal Wickremeratne, Head of Research and Strategy at NDB Securities, said.

“One of the things in the past that were dragging the market down was oil prices and also the negative sentiment globally. I think now some of that sentiment has recovered, you’re seeing oil also coming down, and effectively when you look at Sri Lanka, oil is one of the biggest factors here more than anything else,” Wickremeratne said.

He added that investors were also hopeful that shifts in power in the US House and Senate could lead to potential adjustments in US trade tariffs, providing relief to emerging markets with heavy US tariff burdens.

Positive contributors to the ASPI were Vallibel One (up 6.14 percent at 95.10 rupees), Dialog Axiata (up 4.88 percent at 49.40 rupees), Commercial Bank of Ceylon (up 4.28 percent at 225.25 rupees), Hayleys (up 4.02 percent at 239.25 rupees), and Hatton National Bank (up 3.81 percent at 415.00 rupees).

Softlogic Life Insurance (down 4.98 percent at 78.30 rupees), Softlogic Capital (down 4.17 percent at 11.50 rupees), Ambeon Holdings (down 3.28 percent at 35.40 rupees), LOLC Finance (down 1.96 percent at 5.00 rupees), and Ceylon Cold Stores (down 1.38 percent at 125.00 rupees) were top negative contributors.

Market turnover was 7.96 billion rupees. The banking sector led turnover with 2.03 billion rupees.

Several crossings were recorded during the session, led by Dialog Axiata (800 million rupees), Commercial Bank of Ceylon (309 million rupees), John Keells Holdings (93.7 million rupees), Swisstek (56.1 million rupees), Commercial Credit and Finance (52 million rupees), CAL Closed End Fund (50 million rupees), and Seylan Bank (50 million rupees and 39.2 million rupees).

Other notable crossings included DFCC Bank (41.2 million rupees), D Products (40.8 million rupees), Nations Trust Bank (28.2 million rupees), Ceylon Cold Stores (25 million rupees), CIC Holdings (21.5 million rupees), Hemas Holdings (21.4 million rupees), Sunshine Holdings (21.3 million rupees), Chevron Lubricants Lanka (21 million rupees), and Access Engineering (21 million rupees).

Dialog Axiata generated a combined 1.4 billion rupees of total turnover, driven by 800 million rupees in crossings and over 600 million rupees on the open market. (Colombo/Nov10/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka awards Rs1.73bn contract to build Kelaniya University complex
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: The new building will house the university’s Faculty of Commerce and Management Studies
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT — Sri Lanka’s Cabinet has approved awarding a 1.73 billion rupee contract to M/s Sathuta Builders (Pvt) Ltd to construct a 10-storey building for the University of Kelaniya.

The new building will house the university’s Faculty of Commerce and Management Studies, reviving a project that was earlier halted due to the country’s economic crisis.

The approved contract sum excludes Value Added Tax (VAT).

The procurement began after the Cabinet granted approval on February 3, 2025, to resume the project through national competitive bidding, attracting a total of 10 bids.

“Following the evaluation of the bids, the contract is awarded to the lowest substantially responsive bidder based on recommendations from the procurement committees,” minister Nalinda Jayatissa said. (Colombo/Nov10/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka to build new Mahaweli rail bridge under Indian credit line
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: The historic "Black Bridge" (Kalu Paalama) restoration will proceed in parallel.
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka’s cabinet has approved a proposal to build a new railway bridge across the Mahaweli River between Sarasavi Uyana and Peradeniya, with financial assistance from an Indian credit scheme, minister Nalinda Jayatissa said.

The new bridge on the Matale railway line forms part of an initiative to develop an extensive suburban railway network covering the Kandy municipal area, where a feasibility study is currently underway.

Under the scope of the project, authorities plan to double-track the main railway line from Kadugannawa to Gampola via Peradeniya, and double-track the Matale line from Peradeniya to Katugastota.

Jayatissa noted that these measures are required to complete the planned double-tracking, eliminate bottlenecks caused by existing single-track sections, and improve the reliability and connectivity of the network.

“This project aims to restore and develop railway infrastructure damaged by Cyclone Ditwah and will enable the integration of the Matale railway line into the national railway network,” Jayatissa said.

Responding to questions from reporters on whether the new bridge would halt work on the historic “Black Bridge” (Kalu Paalama), Jayatissa said restoration on the older bridge will proceed in parallel.

“The restoration works will not be stopped,” Jayatissa said. “It is alongside that, that work is being undertaken regarding the construction of this bridge.”

Jayatissa explained that the single-track Black Bridge, originally built in 1865, suffered significant damage during the cyclone.

Due to its age and structural limitations, the Central Engineering Consultancy Bureau (CECB) is carrying out the repairs with technical assistance from the University of Peradeniya.  (Colombo/Nov10/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka to buy 100 Suwa Seriya ambulances with Rs 1.7bn Indian grant
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: New ambulances for the 1990 Suwa Seriya service
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka’s Cabinet of Ministers has approved entering into an agreement with India to secure a financial grant to procure 100 new ambulances for the 1990 Suwa Seriya service, Cabinet Spokesman Nalinda Jayatissa said.

Jayatissa said he presented the proposal to address wear and tear across the emergency fleet.

“As these ambulances cover approximately 9 million kilometers annually, the likelihood of mechanical faults occurring within the existing fleet of 322 ambulances has increased.”

The service operates free of charge 24 hours a day across all districts, handling between 1,000 and 1,200 patient transport requests daily.

Launched in 2016 with Indian financial assistance and expanded island-wide in 2018, the service sought support to replenish aging vehicles.

“In response to a special request made by the Government of Sri Lanka, the Government of India has agreed to provide a financial grant to facilitate the procurement of 100 new ambulances, fully equipped with medical facilities, for use by the ‘1990 Suwasariya’ service.”

Answering questions from journalists on whether the assistance involves debt or restricted procurement, Jayatissa confirmed the funds will arrive as an outright grant rather than a loan.

“It is received as a grant of 1,725.7 million Sri Lankan rupees. It is not a loan; it is received as a grant. Accordingly, tenders will be called for this,” Jayatissa said.

He noted that suppliers will be selected through competitive bidding rather than direct purchase requirements.

Jayatissa added that Sri Lanka’s Ministry of Health will recruit the necessary personnel and manage all maintenance and operations once the funds are released.  (Colombo/Nov10/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka awards Rs9bn in road repair contracts to RR, Maga, ELS
item.dc:creator: Nirmalie Alahakone
item.description: 4 contracts to RR Construction (Pvt) Ltd, Maga Engineering (Pvt) Ltd, ELS Construction (Pvt) Ltd
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka’s Cabinet of Ministers has approved the award of three road development contracts and one post-Ditwah road repair contract worth a combined 9 billion rupees to 3 construction companies, minister Nalinda Jayatissa said.

The contract for widening and improvement of the section from km 62+450 to km 70+000 of the Colombo-Ratnapura-Wellawaya-Batticaloa Road (AA004) was awarded to RR Construction (Pvt) Ltd for 1,485.79 million rupees (inclusive of VAT).

The contract to repair and improve the section from Madampe to km 30+000 (covering km 15+000 to km 30+000) of the Pelmadulla-Embilipitiya-Nonagama Road (A018) was also awarded to RR Construction (Pvt) Ltd for 3,739.84 million rupees (inclusive of VAT).

The contract for widening and improvement of the road section from Haggala Junction to Katugastota (from km 3+000 to km 10+040) of the Peradeniya-Halloluwa-Katugastota Road (B365) was awarded Maga Engineering (Pvt) Ltd for 3,106.21 million rupees (inclusive of VAT).

The contract to repair and improve 3 sections of Nawalapitiya road was awarded to ELS Construction (Pvt) Ltd for 763.98 million rupees (exclusive of Value Added Tax). (Colombo/Nov10/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka’s lost decade: A decade of diverging household incomes
item.dc:creator: Nirmalie Alahakone
item.description: The typical household is worse off despite nominal gains, the Institute of Policy Studies of Sri Lanka (IPS) says
item.content:encoded:
Nearly a decade after 2016, are Sri Lankan households better off? The newly released preliminary results of the Household Income and Expenditure Survey (HIES) 2025 provide an important insight into this question. Despite substantial increases in nominal incomes, the typical Sri Lankan household had less purchasing power in early 2025 than it did nine years earlier, as reported in the 2016 HIES.

More strikingly, the decade has not affected households equally. While real incomes among the poorest households have fallen substantially, those at the upper end of the income distribution have recorded gains that hide the extent of the loss. The widening gap between average and median incomes further suggests that national averages increasingly conceal the experience of the typical household.

Nine Years Without an Improvement in Typical Household Income

According to the Department of Census and Statistics (DCS), average monthly household income increased from Rs. 62,237 in 2016 to Rs. 120,266 in early 2025, an increase of approximately 93%. However, much of this increase reflects inflation rather than improvements in purchasing power.

After adjusting for inflation, real mean household income increased by just 6% over the nine-year period. The experience of the typical household was worse. Real median monthly income fell from Rs. 43,511 in 2016 to Rs. 41,623 in 2025, a 4.3% decline. The comparison between 2016 and 2019 shows that real median household income increased by 7.6%. By early 2025, these gains had disappeared, with real median income falling 11.1% below its 2019 level.

A Lost Decade, but Not for Everyone

The national figures conceal an even more important development: household incomes have followed sharply different trajectories across the income distribution.

After adjusting for inflation, average monthly income among the poorest 20% of households declined from approximately Rs. 14,843 in 2016 to Rs. 12,403 in early 2025, a reduction of 16.4%. In contrast, average real income among the richest 20% increased from approximately Rs. 158,072 to Rs. 184,129, a gain of 16.5%. The divergence is pronounced after 2019, as the COVID-19 pandemic, the economic crisis, and other external shocks produced a decline in real income among the poorest quintile by approximately 19.6%, while income among the richest quintile increased by approximately 6.8% between 2019 and 2025.

Figure: Diverging Real Household Income Trajectories, 2016–2025

Table: Real Monthly Household Income by Income Group, 2016–2025

Sources: Department of Census and Statistics, HIES 2016 and 2019 Final Results, and HIES 2025 Preliminary Results. All real income figures are expressed in 2016 prices.

The average income ratio between the richest and poorest quintiles rose from 10.6 in 2016 to 11.2 in 2019 and 14.8 in early 2025. In other words, the households in the richest quintile earned, on average, nearly 15 times as much as those in the poorest quintile in 2025, compared with approximately 11 times in 2016. These suggest the limited improvement in national average income has concentrated at the top end of the distribution while accompanied by a much weaker experience among households at the lower end of the distribution.

The Growing Distance Between the Average and Typical Household

Another revealing finding is the widening difference between mean and median household income. In 2016, average household income was approximately 43% higher than median income. This relationship remained almost unchanged in 2019. However, by early 2025, average income was nearly 59% higher than median income. The divergence reflects their different trajectories; between 2019 and 2025, real mean household income declined by only 1.7%, while real median income fell by 11.1%.

This suggests the mean is influenced by high incomes, while the median represents the household at the midpoint of the income distribution. As a result, improvements among higher-income households can sustain the national average even when the typical household experiences declining purchasing power. Taken together, the widening mean–median gap and growing richest-to-poorest quintile income ratio point towards an increasingly uneven income distribution. However, these indicators are not substitutes for a comprehensive measure of inequality. The 2019 HIES reported an income Gini coefficient of 0.46, compared with 0.45 in 2016. The forthcoming full HIES 2025 results will be important for establishing whether this broader measure has also changed.

Poverty: The Hidden U-Curve

The latest poverty estimates reinforce concerns about the reversal of earlier progress. Sri Lanka’s poverty headcount declined from 16% in 2016 to 14.3% in 2019. However, the preliminary HIES 2025 findings estimate that poverty returned to 16%. The lack of household data between 2019 and 2025 likely hides a peak in poverty that occurred during that period, as the country experienced a plethora of shocks. The World Bank’s revised estimates suggest poverty may have peaked at around 20% during this period.

Figure: Sri Lanka’s Poverty Trajectory: Crisis and Partial Recovery, 2019–2025

Sources: World Bank (2026), HIES (2019,2025)

Recovering the Economy Must Mean Recovering Household Incomes

Sri Lanka’s return to economic growth is an important achievement. However, the latest HIES results demonstrate why national economic recovery cannot be assessed solely through aggregate indicators. Nearly a decade after 2016, the typical household has lost purchasing power, poverty reduction has returned to its earlier starting point, and income trajectories have diverged substantially between poorer and richer households.

The key question is no longer simply whether Sri Lanka’s economy is recovering, but whether that recovery is reaching households across the income distribution. A sustainable recovery therefore requires more than restoring economic output to transform it into something durable. It must translate into sustained growth in real household earnings, more productive employment opportunities, and greater resilience among economically vulnerable households.

item.title: ADB approves $98mn loan to advance digital transformation in Sri Lanka
item.dc:creator: Nirmalie Alahakone
item.description: It will bolster cybersecurity protection, including monitoring and incident response for government agencies
item.content:encoded:
COLOMBO, SRI LANKA (10 November 2026) — The Asian Development Bank (ADB) has approved a $98 million loan to support Sri Lanka’s efforts to build an inclusive, secure, and resilient digital economy, enhance public service delivery, and strengthen the foundations for private sector-led growth.

The Advancing Digital Transformation Project will help expand high-quality broadband connectivity and improve government data infrastructure, while reinforcing institutional capacity for cybersecurity and data protection and enhancing digital skills across the public sector.

The project aims to boost digital inclusion and equity by expanding access to digital government services for citizens and businesses, particularly women and underserved communities.

ADB is providing an additional $1 million technical assistance grant from its Technical Assistance Special Fund to support program preparation, design, and capacity building for the executing and implementing agencies.

“Sri Lanka has made strong progress in stabilizing its economy and is now prioritizing digital transformation as a key driver of inclusive growth and productivity,” said ADB Country Director for Sri Lanka Shannon Cowlin.

“This project will help bridge connectivity gaps, improve the reliability and security of digital systems, and strengthen institutions to deliver better services to citizens and businesses.”

Despite high mobile coverage, access to reliable, high-speed broadband remains uneven, particularly in rural and underserved areas.

Gaps in digital and data infrastructure, cybersecurity, data protection, and skills continue to constrain the delivery of efficient public services and limit private sector development.

The project will address these challenges through a comprehensive, whole-of-government approach aligned with the government’s National Digital Economy Blueprint.

The project will expand high-quality broadband connectivity in underserved areas; upgrade telecommunications infrastructure and boost services from 2G to 4G and 5G; and make government data systems more reliable, interoperable, and resilient through an enhanced Lanka Government Cloud 3.0.

It will bolster cybersecurity protection, including monitoring and incident response for government agencies deemed as critical national information infrastructure.

It will also improve digital skills to build institutional capacity by training public sector employees, with targeted support to increase women’s participation in the digital economy.

By strengthening digital infrastructure and institutions, the project is expected to improve access to essential services such as health, education, and administrative services, reduce transaction costs, and expand economic opportunities.

It will also enhance resilience by supporting secure, continuous digital systems that are critical to emergency response and service delivery.

item.title: Fitch assigns NDB Wealth Money Fund first-time ‘AA+f(lka)’ and ‘S2(lka)’
item.dc:creator: Nirmalie Alahakone
item.description: The rating also reflects Fitch's treatment of repurchase agreements (repos) with non-investment-grade counterparties,
item.content:encoded:
Fitch Ratings – Colombo: Fitch Ratings has assigned NDB Wealth Money Fund a National Fund Credit Quality Rating (FCQR) of ‘AA+f(lka)’ and a National Fund Market Risk Sensitivity Rating (MRSR) of ‘S2(lka)’.

KEY RATING DRIVERS

The FCQR reflects the high credit quality of the fund’s underlying assets. Fitch bases the rating on the fund’s actual and prospective credit quality. The weighted-average rating factor (WARF) suggested a rating of’ AAAf(lka)’ at end-August 2026. However, the fund’s investment guidelines provide flexibility to invest in money market instruments other than government securities, which could lower the portfolio’s aggregate credit quality. Fitch has therefore assigned the FCQR at ‘AA+f(lka)’.

The MRSR reflects the fund’s low sensitivity to interest-rate and spread risk. The rating also reflects Fitch’s treatment of repurchase agreements (repos) with non-investment-grade counterparties, for which the maturity of the underlying collateral can increase the fund’s calculated market-risk exposure.

ASSET CREDIT QUALITY

The portfolio’s WARF primarily drives the FCQR. The WARF reflects the credit ratings and remaining term to maturity of the securities held in the portfolio, weighted by market value. The fund mainly invests in Sri Lankan government securities, repos backed by Sri Lankan government securities and time deposits with financial institutions. Its WARF at end-August 2026 was 0.15, consistent with an ‘AAAf(lka)’ rating range of 0.0-0.3.

For repos with counterparties unrated by Fitch, Fitch uses the rating and maturity of the collateral in calculating the WARF. Where an investment-grade repo counterparty is rated below the collateral, Fitch uses the collateral rating and the repo contract’s original maturity. The fund’s investment guidelines permit investment in instruments other than government securities, including bank deposits. This flexibility could result in a weaker portfolio WARF than indicated by the current portfolio. The ‘AA+f(lka)’ rating therefore incorporates Fitch’s assessment of both current and prospective portfolio credit quality.

PORTFOLIO SENSITIVITY TO MARKET RISK

Fitch’s proprietary market risk factor (MRF), which measures the fund’s sensitivity to market risk, is within the ‘S2(lka)’ range of 2.0-4.0. The fund’s MRF is higher than its relatively short portfolio maturity might otherwise suggest because, for repos with non-investment-grade counterparties, Fitch incorporates the maturity of the underlying collateral rather than the contractual maturity of the repo. Longer-dated collateral can therefore increase the MRF even where the repo itself is short-dated. This treatment constrains the fund’s MRSR at’S2(lka)’.

FUND PROFILE

The fund, launched in 2012 as the Eagle Money Fund, is an open-end money market fund domiciled in Sri Lanka (Long-Term Issuer Default Rating: B-) and regulated by the country’s Securities and Exchange Commission. It seeks to provide liquidity and above-average returns through investments in short-term government securities and high-credit-quality Sri Lankan rupee-denominated bank deposits. The fund’s assets are segregated and held with its trustee, Hatton National Bank PLC (National Long-Term Rating: AA-(lka)/Stable). The fund’s assets under management (AUM) totaled LKR55 billion at end-August 2026.

INVESTMENT MANAGER

Fitch considers the investment manager, NDB Wealth Management Limited, to be a suitably qualified, competent and capable of managing the fund. The company was incorporated in 1992 as CTC Eagle Fund Management Company Limited. It was renamed Eagle NDB Fund Management Company Limited. in 1997 and NDB Aviva Wealth Management Limited in 2009, before adopting its current name in 2013.

NDB Wealth Management is a subsidiary of NDB Capital Holdings Limited, which is ultimately owned by National Development Bank PLC (NDB) . NDB owns around 99.9% of NDB Capital Holdings, which in turn owns about 99.99% of NDB Wealth Management. The remaining minority interest is held by a sister company.

NDB Wealth Management is licensed by the Securities and Exchange Commission of Sri Lanka as a unit trust management company and investment manager. It manages unit trusts across money market, equity, fixed-income and sharia-compliant strategies, as well as discretionary investment portfolios for institutional and individual clients.

NDB Wealth Management is Sri Lanka’s second-largest asset manager, with mutual fund AUM of LKR145 billion as of end-September 2026, representing 25% of the country’s mutual funds market. The company manages three money market funds (50% of AUM), two income funds (46%) and one equity fund (2%) one balanced fund (2%) and one gilt-edged fund (0%).

RATING SENSITIVITIES

Factors that Could, Individually or Collectively, Lead to Negative Rating Action/Downgrade
The ratings may be sensitive to significant changes in the fund’s credit quality or market-risk profile. A large, adverse deviation from Fitch’s guidelines for any key rating driver could lead to a downgrade.

The FCQR could be downgraded if the fund materially increases exposure to lower-credit-quality assets, resulting in a sustained deterioration in its WARF.

The MRSR could be downgraded if the fund materially increases its duration or its exposure to repos with non-investment-grade counterparties backed by longer-dated collateral, resulting in a higher MRF.

Factors that Could, Individually or Collectively, Lead to Positive Rating Action/Upgrade
The FCQR could be upgraded if the fund maintains portfolio credit quality consistent with a higher rating on a sustained basis, including a stable allocation to higher-credit-quality assets.

The MRSR could be upgraded if the fund’s market-risk profile declines sufficiently for its MRF to be sustained within the range consistent with a higher MRSR.

item.title: Sri Lanka posts Rs22.3bn budget surplus in Jan-Sep 2026
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: Mainly due to the significant increase in government revenue by 20 percent, together with the rationalization of governm
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka recorded an overall budget surplus of 22.3 billion rupees in the first nine months of 2026, shifting from a deficit of 441.4 billion rupees in the same period of 2025, according to the Fiscal Review Report (January – September 2026) published by the Ministry of Finance.

The fiscal turnaround was driven by a sharp 20 percent expansion in state receipts — buoyed heavily by motor vehicle import duties — alongside restrained public spending growth.

“The budget surplus of Rs. 22.3 billion was recorded mainly due to the significant increase in government revenue by 20 percent, together with the rationalization of government expenditure,” the report said.

Total government revenue and grants rose to 4,601.6 billion rupees between January and September 2026, up from 3,834.9 billion rupees a year earlier.

This reached 86.8 percent of the government’s full-year target of 5,300 billion rupees.

Tax revenue alone increased 19.3 percent to 4,252.1 billion rupees.

Sri Lanka Customs and the Inland Revenue Department (IRD) were the primary contributors, each accounting for 47 percent of total tax receipts.

Vehicle import boost

Sri Lanka Customs brought in 1,981 billion rupees, achieving 89.8 percent of its annual target.

Import Value Added Tax (VAT) rose 14 percent to 690.3 billion rupees, while Customs-collected excise duty rose 15 percent to 636.1 billion rupees.

Within excise duties, vehicle collections climbed 9.1 percent to 381.0 billion rupees, making up 60 percent of total Customs excise earnings.

“Sri Lanka Customs achieved 90 percent of its annual estimate in the first nine months of 2026 mainly due to the increase of revenue collection from import of motor vehicles.”

Domestically, the IRD collected 2,014 billion rupees, meeting 83.9 percent of its target.

Income tax collections rose 20 percent to 996.4 billion rupees, while domestic VAT collections expanded by 29 percent.

Expenditure and growth

Total government spending grew at a controlled rate of 7.1 percent to 4,579.3 billion rupees.

Recurrent expenditure rose 5.6 percent to 4,036.6 billion rupees.

Interest payments, which formed 45 percent of recurrent spending, fell 5 percent to 1,821.6 billion rupees from 1,906.6 billion rupees in 2025.

Meanwhile, capital and net lending rose 19.2 percent to 542.8 billion rupees.

The primary surplus widened to 1,843.9 billion rupees from 1,465.1 billion rupees recorded a year earlier.

The report also noted that economic growth moderated to 4.2 percent in the second quarter of 2026, compared to 5.0 percent in the second quarter of 2025.  (Colombo/Nov10/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka to fast-track 10MW waste-to-energy plant in Ja-Ela
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: Officials said the project will play a role in local disaster prevention by stopping discarded waste from clogging canal
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT — Sri Lanka is moving to fast-track a 10-megawatt (MW) waste-to-energy project in Ja-Ela under a public-private partnership (PPP) model to resolve the garbage crisis in the Gampaha District and feed renewable energy into the national grid, officials said.

The proposed facility, located in Suduwella, is designed to strengthen waste management across the Western Province while converting municipal waste into usable power.

Feasibility studies assessing the project’s hydrological, social, environmental, and legal aspects have already been completed, officials said.

Authorities hope to secure recommendations from the National Planning Department (NPD) and finalize grid connection procedures before submitting a Cabinet paper for approval.

Officials said the project will play a role in local disaster prevention by stopping discarded waste from clogging canals and natural drainage paths.

Last week the capital city went under water within a couple of hours of rain as Colombo’s drains were not cleared despite anticipated showers. (Colombo/Nov10/2026)

item.title: Softlogic Life Insurance Sept quarter net profit plunges 93-pct to Rs76.5mn
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: Profitability was heavily weighed down by a 34.2 percent rise in total benefits, claims, and expenses to Rs. 13.20 bn
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT — Sri Lanka’s Softlogic Life Insurance PLC recorded a group net profit of Rs. 76.5 million for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, plunging 92.9 percent from Rs. 1.07 billion in the same quarter last year, interim accounts showed.

The group posted basic earnings per share of Rs. 0.24 for the September quarter, down from Rs. 3.38 a year earlier.

Quarterly gross written premiums (GWP) expanded 18.1 percent to Rs. 12.25 billion from Rs. 10.38 billion, while net written premiums grew 17.3 percent to Rs. 11.34 billion after ceding Rs. 906.7 million to reinsurers.

Total other revenue rose 17.6 percent to Rs. 2.01 billion from Rs. 1.71 billion, bolstered by a 30.5 percent jump in net finance income to Rs. 1.93 billion.

However, net realised investment gains dropped to Rs. 13.5 million from Rs. 96.9 million, and net fair value gains softened to Rs. 62.4 million from Rs. 77.6 million.

Total net revenue advanced 17.4 percent to Rs. 13.35 billion from Rs. 11.38 billion.

Despite steady top-line growth, profitability was heavily weighed down by a 34.2 percent rise in total benefits, claims, and expenses to Rs. 13.20 billion.

The sharp bottom-line contraction was primarily driven by a nearly threefold increase in the change in insurance contract liabilities, which rose to Rs. 2.81 billion from Rs. 955.7 million a year earlier.

Financial statement notes revealed that while Rs. 1.28 billion in surplus was transferred from the non-participating life fund to shareholders during the first half of the year, no surplus transfer was recognized in the September quarter.

Net insurance benefits and claims paid rose 22.2 percent to Rs. 6.07 billion, while underwriting and net acquisition costs inched up 3.2 percent to Rs. 2.03 billion.

Other operating and administrative expenses climbed 16.3 percent to Rs. 2.05 billion.

The quarter marked the group’s initial consolidation of Bangladesh-based Diamond Life Insurance Company Limited, following the acquisition of a 60 percent controlling stake for Rs. 641.5 million on July 1.

Finance costs jumped 92.6 percent to Rs. 300.7 million, driven by higher interest expenses after the group drew long-term borrowings during the period, lifting total borrowings to Rs. 4.89 billion from zero at the end of 2025.

Pre-tax profit fell 90.4 percent to Rs. 147.9 million from Rs. 1.54 billion, while income tax expense declined 84.8 percent to Rs. 71.4 million.

Total assets reached Rs. 81.89 billion as of September 30, up from Rs. 68.59 billion in December 2025.

Net asset value per share stood at Rs. 39.98, or Rs. 35.19 excluding the restricted regulatory one-off surplus reserve.

Softlogic Life stock was trading at 79.50 rupees. (Colombo/Nov10/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka worker remittances up 3.3-pct to US$735.6mn in Sept; likely record high in 2026
item.dc:creator: Shihar Aneez
item.description: Analysts expect remittances to be in the range of US$9bn in 2026
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka’s official remittances from expatriate workers rose 3.3 percent to US$ 735.6 million in October 2026, official data showed, while they are expected to hit fresh record high in November, analysts said.

The total remittances in the first 10 months of the year reached US$7,600.9 million with a 16.5 percent growth, Central Bank data showed.

Analysts said Sri Lanka will see record high remittances this month, surpassing the historically high annual worker remittance of US$8,076.2 million hit in 2025. They predict the remittances to reach near US$9 billion by end of this year, if the same economic and exchange rate policies continue in Sri Lanka.

The remittances hit a seven-month low in June following the rupee’s depreciation after escalation in the Middle East, the largest foreign job market for Sri Lankans. They have recovered since then.

The rupee has been largely stable and showed a slight appreciating trend since July though it has shown some downside pressure since in the last two months, currency dealers say.

When there is uncertainty over the exchange rate, market analysts say expatriates switch to informal remittance methods like Hawala and Undiyal, which do not go through the formal banking system.

The island nation saw a record monthly remittance of US$879.1 million in December last year.

Higher worker remittances follow a higher number of the island nation’s labour force leaving the country to search for foreign jobs amid Sri Lanka’s recovery from an unprecedented 2022 economic crisis, official data showed.

A total of 211,666 Sri Lankan workers have departed the country for overseas employment during the first nine months of 2026, Sri Lanka Bureau of Foreign Employment (SLBFE) has said.

Remittances have risen continuously after the central bank abandoned a parallel exchange rate regime in 2022, which compelled most expatriates to switch from informal Undiyal and Hawala money transfer methods.

The island nation has been in the process of sending more migrant workers focusing on professionals to bring in higher foreign exchange since the country declared bankruptcy in 2022.

Worker remittances through official channels fell sharply in 2021 after many expatriates switched to informal money transferring channels because they were offered higher rates than formal banking channels.

The move followed the Central Bank printing money to sterilize interventions and keep a policy rate down, which triggered parallel exchange rates settled outside the formal banking system.

From April 2022, the interest rates were raised by unprecedented levels, slowing credit and the need to print money to keep rates down. Later, the Central Bank started its dovish monetary policy until May this year. (Colombo/November 10/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka’s flash floods in capital point to systemic institutional failure, ignored directives
item.dc:creator: Shihar Aneez
item.description: PM Harini Amarasuriya on Oct 13 instructed officials to clean Colombo’s canal, drainage systems within 2 weeks
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – As torrential monsoon downpours transformed Sri Lanka’s commercial capital’s thoroughfares into raging brown rivers on Friday (06) submerging vehicles, paralyzing public transit, and inundating critical facilities like the National Hospital, the crisis was framed by authorities as an act of nature.

But for the millions of residents wading through waist-deep water, the disaster was not merely meteorological. It was man-made, preventable, and a glaring testament to gross institutional negligence.

Vraîe Cally Balthazaar, the Mayor of the island nation’s biggest local governing body Colombo Municipal Council (CMC) posted on her FaceBook (Meta) platform just a week ago before the floods that people in her ward “have had to live with the risk of flooding for years” after the stormwater drain running through the Jawatta Public Cemetery collapsed in 2019.

She said in the post that she promised the residents that the CMC would get the repairs done before the end of September, and she was happy to say that the CMC has “managed to complete the work by September 15.

“And sometimes, something as simple as fixing a drain can make a real difference to an entire neighbourhood,” Balthazaar said.

However, the flash floods saw the same area heavily flooded despite the ‘fixing’ by the CMC.

Just 24 days before the floods, Prime Minister Harini Amarasuriya herself issued a direct, unequivocal order to government officials and municipal authorities to treat the cleaning of Colombo’s canal and drainage systems as an exceptional priority.

She directed to expedite the work and complete it within two weeks to ensure proper rainwater management amid anticipated increases in rainfall.

Prime Minister Amarasuriya issued these directives while addressing the Colombo District Coordinating Committee meeting held on October 13 at the Narahenpita District Secretariat.

During the meeting, officials from divisional secretariat offices, the Agrarian Development Department, and the Provincial Irrigation Department highlighted existing challenges in cleaning drainage and canal systems, noting issues such as a shortage of technical officers and difficulties faced in formulating plans and estimates.

Her instruction came in response to early meteorological indicators pointing toward an intensifying inter-monsoonal rainfall season.

But the floods last week proved that these directives had been ignored, delayed, and left unimplemented by the very bodies sworn to protect the city’s populace.

Recognizing the chronic vulnerability of the commercial capital’s low-lying geography, the Prime Minister instructed relevant stakeholders to systematically clear Colombo’s primary canals, secondary outlets, and subterranean drainage systems.

Crucially, the directive came with a strict deadline: a two-week window to complete the comprehensive clearing of blockages, silt, and solid waste that choke the city’s waterways.

Colombo would not have had last week’s floods, had the Prime Minister’s instruction been heeded and executed.

But the Prime Minister’s instruction designed precisely to preempt the catastrophic urban flooding that has chronically plagued Colombo during heavy weather was ignored.

Yet, when the skies opened up last Friday (06), the two-week deadline had long expired into the ether of bureaucratic inaction.

The canals remained congested with plastic debris, unauthorized construction bottlenecks, and thick layers of silt.

The drainage systems, starved of maintenance, failed instantly.

Neither the central government machinery nor the Colombo Municipal Council (CMC) can wash their hands of accountability.

The ‘Clean Sri Lanka’ programme under the current government has been created to deal with prevention of flooding among many other ambitious goals.

“The responsibility for this damage must be borne by the President even more than the Mayor,” former Urban Development and Megapolis Minister Champika Ranawaka, a strong government critic, said on his YouTube platform.

“He is the head of the disaster management apparatus, and ‘Clean Sri Lanka’ operates under his direct leadership. Because of his actions and their administrative conduct, the entire state machinery has been brought to a standstill.”

Anatomy of Municipal Paralysis

When orders from the higher office like Prime Minister of the state can be casually sidelined by municipal inertia, it exposes a profound fracture in governance, one where public safety is compromised by institutional paralysis.

At the heart of Colombo’s drainage crisis is a systemic failure of local governance and inter-agency coordination.

The Colombo Municipal Council, tasked with the day-to-day stewardship of municipal infrastructure, waste management, and local drainage networks, has long operated in an administrative comfort zone characterized by reactive posturing rather than proactive mitigation.

When the Prime Minister’s directive was issued in mid-October, it should have triggered an immediate emergency mobilization.

Municipal work crews, heavy machinery, and desilting operations ought to have been deployed across every vulnerable ward, from the commercial hubs of Fort and Pettah to densely populated residential quarters like Borella, Wellawatte, and Grandpass.

Instead, citizens witnessed what can only be described as administrative inertia.

Bureaucratic red tape, sluggish procurement of maintenance contracts, and a lack of accountability mechanisms meant that instructions from the Prime Minister trickled down into endless committee meetings rather than field operations.

By treating a critical pre-monsoon cleanup as a routine administrative task rather than an urgent, life-saving imperative, municipal officials displayed a reckless disregard for urban risk management.

The government repeatedly said it has collected ample tax revenue to run the country. But that money could not be used urgently to protect the Colombo city when it was evident what was going to happen as per Prime Minister Amarasuriya’s instructions.

Furthermore, the failure extends beyond mere delayed cleanups to encompass chronic structural enforcement failures.

Over decades, Colombo’s natural hydrological buffers including its wetlands, marshes, and secondary flood retention areas have been systematically degraded or encroached upon by uncoordinated commercial and residential developments.

When drainage systems are clogged with garbage while vital retention pathways are blocked by concrete, even a standard heavy downpour is bound to trigger catastrophe.

Friday’s deluge merely exposed the cumulative cost of this willful administrative blindness.

Economic Toll of Negligence

The consequences of this systemic failure were borne immediately by ordinary citizens and critical public infrastructure.

The inundation of the National Hospital of Sri Lanka, where floodwaters unprecedentedly breached critical service areas, should be considered a national scandal.

That a premier healthcare institution can be crippled within 2 hours of heavy rain, jeopardizing patient care and compromising sterile environments, illustrates the deadly stakes of municipal failure.

Beyond the hospitals, small business owners watched their livelihoods float away, commuters were stranded for hours in gridlocked, submerged buses, and low-income families residing in underserved settlements suffered extensive property damage.

For an urban economy trying to anchor Sri Lanka’s fragile post-crisis recovery, recurring paralyzing floods exact a heavy toll in lost productivity, infrastructure damage, and emergency response costs.

Accountability

The CMC and government have pointed fingers at the illegal structures erected under past governments for the latest disaster. But this government has already been in power for two years.

In the aftermath of the disaster, routine finger-pointing between central agencies and municipal bodies also has begun, with officials attempting to deflect blame onto unprecedented rainfall volumes.

But meteorological data offers no refuge for negligent administrators.

The rainfall, while heavy, was seasonally anticipated; indeed, it was precisely why the Prime Minister issued her October directive.

When a directive issued by the second-in-command of the country is left gathering dust on a municipal desk while citizens face preventable devastation, the social contract breaks down.

The current government and the Colombo Municipal Council cannot hide behind excuses of resource constraints or administrative oversight.

Preventing flash floods requires more than issuing seasonal press releases or convening post-disaster committees after the water has receded.

It demands rigorous enforcement, transparent institutional accountability, and a zero-tolerance approach to administrative lethargy.

If the authorities cannot execute basic drainage maintenance, Colombo will remain structurally vulnerable, hostage to the next raincloud, and failed by the very institutions meant to protect it. (Colombo/November 08/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka’s Hayleys Retail to launch supermarket chain with Blue Yonder
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: “With Blue Yonder, our teams will have AI-driven insight to deliver a seamless, consistent shopping experience
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT — Hayleys Retail Holdings Ltd has selected supply chain software provider Blue Yonder to build its grocery retail operations from the ground up, the two companies said in a joint statement.

Hayleys Retail, a member of Sri Lanka’s diversified conglomerate Hayleys Group, plans to open several stores across the country. The agreement marks Blue Yonder’s first retail customer in Sri Lanka.

“Our entry into supermarket retail is about bringing that same commitment to quality and reliability closer to everyday Sri Lankan consumers,” Mohan Pandithage, Chairman and Chief Executive of Hayleys PLC said.

“With Blue Yonder, our teams will have AI-driven insight to deliver a seamless, consistent shopping experience across every store,” he said.

Hayleys, which accounts for approximately 5 percent of Sri Lanka’s export income and operates across 17 business sectors, is entering the large-scale supermarket space by drawing on its group strengths in manufacturing, logistics, and services.

The company selected Blue Yonder to connect its data across merchandising and shelf space, deploy artificial intelligence agents to catch operational issues early, and scale its business into a national network without changing platforms.

The rollout will begin with merchandise operations to manage suppliers, items, costs, and pricing, followed by machine learning capabilities to forecast demand and balance store inventory during seasonal peaks.

“Hayleys Retail is choosing one where AI is the foundation rather than an add-on—connected data and agentic AI built into core merchandising operations, and planning that learns as the business grows,” Antonio Boccalandro, President, APAC at Blue Yonder said.

The retailer plans to use the platform to automate routine store tasks and adjust inventory according to real-time sales and local market trends as its store footprint grows. (Colombo/Nov09/2026)
